'''Vincent Lamar Wilfork''' (born November 4, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive tackle]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 13 seasons, primarily with the [[New England Patriots]]. He is regarded as one of the greatest defensive tackles of all time.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://archive.boston.com/sports/football/patriots/articles/2008/11/28/hes_one_of_the_best/|title=He's one of the best|work=[[The Boston Globe]]|first=Christopher L.|last=Gasper|date=November 28, 2008|access-date=May 20, 2009|archive-date=February 11, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090211232304/http://www.boston.com/sports/football/patriots/articles/2008/11/28/hes_one_of_the_best/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/football/nfl/2008-07-05-top-five-defensive-tackles_N.htm|title=Best run stuffer? Finding the best defensive tackle in the NFL|work=[[USA Today]]|date=July 6, 2008|access-date=May 20, 2009|archive-date=January 7, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120107160718/http://www.usatoday.com/sports/football/nfl/2008-07-05-top-five-defensive-tackles_N.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>

Wilfork played [[college football]] for the [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]], earning first-team All-[[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East]] honors in 2003. He was selected in the first round of the [[2004 NFL draft]] by the Patriots, where he spent his first 11 seasons. During his New England tenure, Wilfork received five [[Pro Bowl]] selections and one first-team [[All-Pro]] selection.<ref>{{cite web |title=Vince Wilfork Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WilfVi20.htm |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |access-date=February 20, 2024 |language=en |archive-date=January 16, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240116131414/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WilfVi20.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Wilfork also won two [[Super Bowl]] titles. In his final two seasons, Wilfork was a member of the [[Houston Texans]].

'''Victor Allan Riley''' (November 4, 1974 – April 8, 2024) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Riley played [[college football]] for the [[Auburn Tigers football|Auburn Tigers]]. He was selected in the first round of the [[1998 NFL draft]] by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]], with whom he played for four seasons.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1998 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1998/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was the No. 7 offensive tackle available in the draft, according to ''[[Sports Illustrated]]''.<ref>[https://archive.today/20130215174831/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/events/1998/nfldraft/topplayers/byposition/OT.html sportsillustrated.cnn.com] </ref> He also played for three seasons with the [[New Orleans Saints]] before signing in 2005 with the [[Houston Texans]]. Riley died in [[Swansea, South Carolina]] on April 8, 2024, at the age of 49.<ref>{{cite news |title=Former New Orleans Saints tackle Victor Riley transitions at 49 |url=https://www.neworleanssaints.com/news/victor-riley-new-orleans-saints-tackle-dead-49-chiefs-texans-auburn |access-date=12 April 2024 |publisher=New Orleans Saints |date=11 April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Victor Riley Obituary (1974–2024) | website=Legacy.com | date=2024-04-18 | url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/thestate/name/victor-riley-obituary?id=54898846 | access-date=2025-08-16}}</ref>

'''Vincent Tobias Evans''' (born June 14, 1955) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]] and was the [[most valuable player]] (MVP) of the [[1977 Rose Bowl]] after the team's 14–6 victory over [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan]]. He was selected by the [[Chicago Bears]] in the sixth round of the [[1977 NFL draft]].

Evans played professionally for the Bears as well as Chicago's team in the [[United States Football League]] (USFL), the [[Chicago Blitz]], as well as the USFL's [[Denver Gold]], and the NFL's [[Los Angeles Raiders|Los Angeles]]/[[Oakland Raiders]] in a career that spanned nearly 20 years from 1977 to 1995.

'''Vincent Cole Brisby''' (born January 25, 1971) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for the [[New England Patriots]] and the [[New York Jets]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).<ref name="nflprofile">{{cite web | url=http://www.nfl.com/player/vincentbrisby/2499788/profile | title=Vincent Brisby, WR | publisher=National Football League | work=NFL.com | access-date=August 17, 2014}}</ref> He was selected by the Patriots in the second round of the [[1993 NFL draft]], the team's fourth selection after quarterback [[Drew Bledsoe]], DL [[Chris Slade (American football)|Chris Slade]], and OL [[Todd Rucci]] during their re-building phase that started with the hiring of [[Bill Parcells]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1993 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1993/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Standing at 6'3" and 193 lb. from [[Northeast Louisiana University]] (now called University of Louisiana at Monroe), Brisby played eight NFL seasons from 1993 to 2000 for the Patriots and [[New York Jets]]. He was given the nickname Vincent "[[Ultimate frisbee|Ultimate]]" Brisby by [[ESPN]] analyst [[Chris Berman]]. Brisby's best game was arguably Week 5 in his second season. He compiled 6 catches for 117 yards and two touchdowns in the Patriots 17–16 comeback win over the Green Bay Packers.

Brisby was a member of the Patriots' 1996 AFC Championship squad. He injured his hamstring in pre-season that year and did not get into a game until Week 12, then missed two more games at which point his coach Bill Parcells was memorably quoted as saying that he himself had "recovered from open-heart surgery faster than he (Brisby) has (from the hamstring injury)...That's the truth. I'm not kidding you." After playing in only three regular season games and catching no passes at all in the regular season, divisional play-off, or AFC Championship, Brisby had two catches against the [[Green Bay Packers]] in [[Super Bowl XXXI]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XXXI - New England Patriots vs. Green Bay Packers - January 26th, 1997 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199701260gnb.htm |access-date=2025-10-18 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>
